subdivision.heading: Assessment of Costs by Assessment Officer

operative_text.controlling:
10.38(1)  For the purpose of assessing costs payable, an
assessment officer may do all or any of the following:
(a) take evidence either by affidavit or orally under oath, or
both;
(b) direct the production of records;
(c) require notice of the appointment for the assessment to be
served on persons who may be affected by the assessment
or who have an interest in the trust, estate, fund or
property from which the costs are or may be paid or
charged;
(d) give directions about how a notice of the appointment for
the assessment is to be served;
(e) allow a party to be independently represented by a lawyer;
(f) require details of the services provided and disbursements
or other charges claimed or require information about any
other matter necessary to understand the reason for an
item in the bill of costs and to decide whether the item and
charge is reasonable and proper;
(g) validate service of the notice of the appointment or, if
service is impractical or impossible, dispense with service.
(2)  An assessment officer may not conduct an assessment of costs
that have previously been assessed by an assessment officer unless
the Court so orders or the parties agree.

BOOK_A.title: Assessment Ofﬁcer’s Authority
BOOK_A.related_provisions: 10.17 (review officer’s authority) ; 10.43(2) (certificate is conclusive proof of amount assessed); 11.27 (validating service) ; 11.29 (dispensing with service)
BOOK_A.commentary:
On the general principles of regulating party-party costs, see Alta. Treas. case.¹
A Review Ofﬁcer hearing a dispute about a legal bill has power to take evidence, even unsworn
evidence. An allegation that the retainer (for an hourly charge) had been suspended and that
further work was free, is a dispute about amount, and does not need a reference to the court
under R.10.18(1) (a).²
Under Rr.10.38 and 10.39 the assessment ofﬁcer can make a reference to the court for a
decision or direction on the reasonableness of costs or level of costs, and this was done and
commented on by the referee (a Master).³
At one time a certiﬁcate of disbursements was needed, but even then its absence was not fatal,
and was readily curable if receipts are available, as they are better evidence and the assessment
ofﬁcer can (and often does) look at them.⁴
After 2010, a Master (as referee) held that invoices or
other proof of disbursements should automatically be provided with the proposed bill of costs.⁵
The review ofﬁcer cannot decide the terms of a retainer agreement, including how to interprete
it, nor decide on implied retainer agreements; they must go to a judge to decide, if contested.⁶

BOOK_B.title: Assessment officer's authority

commentary.text: Rule 10.38 See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 10.38. In Equitable Bank v. Avison, 2015 ABQB 109, 2015 CarswellAlta 222 (Master), Master Schulz said, at paragraph 38: 38 The Court relies on the assessment officer to perform this function for the smooth and efficient processing of all litigation matters, and foreclosures in particular. Counsel must keep this function in mind and comply with reasonable requests from the assessment officer to provide records or details of the services or disbursements claimed. Many of the matters raised at the Rule 9.35(4) application before me could have been avoided if the documentation had been provided to the assessment officer when requested, rather than requiring a direction from the Court to do so. When Counsel disagree with the request or position of the assessment officer, Counsel should avoid using aggressive language whether in writing or in person. The assessment officer is an officer of the Court and must be treated respectfully. Counsel must also remember that the Court will not make orders unless there is affidavit or other evidence properly before it. When the matter reaches the point of being reviewed by the Court, it will often require items to be in affidavit form that the assessment officer does not. Remember that “you get more flies with honey than you do with vinegar”.

BOOK_C.title: Assessment officer’s authority

commentary.text:
The assessment officer, as adjudicator of costs payable, is granted a number of powers under this rule to permit them to discharge their function.
The court relies on the assessment officer to perform this function for the smooth and efficient processing of all litigation matters, and foreclosures in particular. Counsel must keep this function in mind and comply with reasonable requests from the assessment officer to provide records or details of the services or disbursements claimed. Equitable Bank v. Avison, [2015] A.J. No. 166, 2015 ABQB 109 at para. 38 (Alta. Q.B. (Master)).
